Operations: who runs what, runbooks, open decisions

Published

September 30, 2026

This page is for whoever has to keep bioconductor.org running on the new stack. How a request is answered and how content is published is on how bioconductor.org works; this page covers who operates each part, what to do when something breaks, what is waiting on a decision, and the biggest risks. Facts here were checked on 2026-09-30.

Who operates what

One person operates the new stack: Sean Davis (seandavi@gmail.com). No backup operator is named anywhere. If Sean Davis is unavailable, nobody else has documented access to the Cloudflare account, the sync host, or the credentials the sync uses.

Component Where it runs Operated by How a failure is noticed
bioconductor.org DNS zone, bioc-site Worker, R2 bucket bioc-site Cloudflare, on a personal account. Moving to a Bioconductor account is deferred Sean Davis bioc-edge health.yml, daily, from GitHub Actions
Registrar and the Route53 zone kept as the DNS rollback target AWS Not recorded on this site None
bioc-sync (hourly), bioc-reconcile (weekly, Sunday 04:00) systemd user units on onclappc02, running from the dev checkout ~/Documents/git/bioc-edge Sean Davis A GitHub issue in bioc-edge titled bioc-sync.service is failing (or bioc-reconcile…), opened or commented on by bioc-notify@
bioc-logpush-check (daily 07:15 local) systemd user unit on onclappc02, from ~/Documents/git/bioc-traffic Sean Davis The same bioc-notify@ issue in bioc-edge
Site build and publish (site/<sha>, site/latest) bioc-website GitHub Actions, on every push to main Sean Davis The site badge
Site data snapshot (_ci/site-data.tar.zst: prose and package data the build reads) R2. Prose and assets refreshed by bioc-site-refresh on every upstream push; package data by hand Sean Davis bioc-site-refresh failures open an issue; stale package data fails no check
bioc-registry Worker (not in the serving path) Cloudflare, deployed by hand with wrangler deploy Sean Davis bioc-registry freshness.yml, daily
master.bioconductor.org and the Bioconductor Build System (BBS) Legacy servers Bioconductor core team bioc-edge parity.yml compares production with master daily

The failure notices go to one GitHub issue per unit; a repeat failure adds a comment rather than a new issue. Nothing closes the issue when the unit recovers, so close it by hand. The notices run on onclappc02 itself, so if that host is down no issue is filed; only the daily GitHub Actions checks still run. Every scheduled job and its badge is listed in CI & scheduled jobs.

Credentials for the sync and purge scripts come from Secret Manager into a gitignored .env in the bioc-edge checkout (./make-env.sh). Splitting the production units away from dev checkouts, and automating detection and routine fixes, is planned in bioc-infrastructure#43.

Runbooks

All commands run from the bioc-edge checkout on onclappc02 unless stated. For commands that call the Cloudflare API, load the credentials first:

./make-env.sh && set -a && . ./.env && set +a

None of these procedures has been rehearsed on production as a drill. The M1 item “Rollback rehearsed and written up” is still open on the roadmap.

Deploy the Worker

Deploys are manual; there is no deploy from CI yet (an open M0 item).

  1. Note the version that is live now, so you can return to it: cd worker && npx wrangler deployments list
  2. Deploy: just deploy-worker (runs npx wrangler deploy in worker/). The routes come from worker/wrangler.jsonc, and a deploy replaces the Worker’s routes with that list, so a route added in the dashboard disappears on the next deploy.
  3. Check: curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep -iE '^server|cf-cache-status|x-bioc-build' shows server: cloudflare, and a package index still answers: curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/src/contrib/PACKAGES.
  4. Run the probe now rather than waiting for tomorrow’s: gh workflow run health.yml -R seandavi/bioc-edge.

Roll back the Worker

  1. cd worker && npx wrangler deployments list and pick the last good version ID.
  2. npx wrangler rollback <version-id> -m "<reason>".
  3. Check as in step 3 above. A rollback changes which Worker version runs; R2 content, _routes.json and the edge cache are untouched.

Roll back the site build

The Worker serves whichever build _routes.json names. "latest" follows the site/latest pointer that bioc-website CI moves on every main build.

  1. Find the last good build sha: gh run list -R seandavi/bioc-website -w site.yml -b main (each successful run published site/<headSha>/).

  2. Write the route table with that sha pinned:

    echo '{"build": "<good sha>", "prefixes": ["/"]}' > routes.json
npx wrangler r2 object put bioc-site/_routes.json --file routes.json --remote

  3. Within about a minute, curl -sI https://bioconductor.org/ | grep x-bioc-build shows the pinned sha. No purge is needed: build pages are cached under their build’s sha.

  4. To undo, write {"build": "latest", "prefixes": ["/"]} the same way. While the pin is in place, new main builds publish but are not served.

An empty prefixes list, or no _routes.json, makes the mirror serve everything: the legacy pages copied from master. That is the fallback if no build is good.

A failed sync

A failed bioc-sync opens (or comments on) the issue bioc-sync.service is failing in bioc-edge, with the run’s journal and log files.

  1. Read the issue, or journalctl --user -u bioc-sync.service -n 100.
  2. If rsync failed (the log says “aborting before touching R2”), nothing in R2 changed. Fix the cause (the log and .err file say what rsync hit), then run one now: systemctl --user start bioc-sync.service. Rsync exits 23 and 24 (unreadable or vanished files) are expected and do not fail the run.
  3. If the run failed after uploading started, the next run does not retry files it already pulled. Run the checksum pass, which reports what is missing or different in R2 and prints the rclone copy command that re-uploads it: systemctl --user start bioc-reconcile.service. It hashes the whole local mirror and takes hours (the unit allows 12); it holds the mirror lock, so hourly syncs skip while it runs.
  4. If the purge step failed, the files are in R2 but the edge may still serve old copies. Purge the keys from the run’s log (below).
  5. When a run succeeds (systemctl --user status bioc-sync.service), close the issue.

A missed hour is caught up by the timer (Persistent=true). bioc-reconcile failing to get the lock within two hours also files an issue.

Purge the edge cache

The hourly sync purges what it changes, so a manual purge is for when that did not happen.

. ./cf-purge.sh
cf_purge_keys packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/PACKAGES   # storage keys: 3.23, not release

cf_purge_keys purges each key on all four hosts in both zones. Check with curl -sI for cf-cache-status: MISS. The rate limit is shared with the running sync; read Purging on the edge-cache page before purging more than a few hundred URLs or a whole zone.

Pull a bad package

The mirror in R2 follows master: the hourly sync copies master with deletions, so a file removed from master is deleted from R2 and purged on the next run, together with the updated PACKAGES. The lasting fix is removing the package on master, which is the core team’s BBS process, not something this stack controls.

If users must stop receiving the file before that happens:

  1. Delete each copy from R2 by its storage key (numeric version, not release; source tarball and each binary are separate keys): rclone delete r2:bioc-site/packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/<pkg>_<ver>.tar.gz
  2. Purge the same keys: cf_purge_keys packages/3.23/bioc/src/contrib/<pkg>_<ver>.tar.gz.
  3. Check the URL returns 404.

What this does and does not do, from how sync.sh works (checked 2026-09-30; not yet done on production):

  • PACKAGES still lists the package until master’s index changes, so installs fail with a download error instead of installing the bad file.
  • The hourly sync uploads only files that changed on master, so it does not put the file back unless master’s copy changes. The weekly reconcile will list it as missing from R2; do not run the re-upload command it prints for that key.
  • Mirrors that already synced the file keep it.

Roll back DNS

The Route53 zone and CloudFront are kept as the rollback target, and records are frozen until 2026-10-12: change no DNS record in either zone, or make the same change in both.

  • The Worker is the problem, DNS is fine: switch the bioconductor.org and www records to DNS only in the Cloudflare dashboard. Traffic goes straight to CloudFront and the legacy servers within 300 s. Steps: flip the site, rollback.
  • Cloudflare’s DNS service is the problem: put the Route53 nameservers back at the registrar. Most resolvers follow within an hour, some take a day. Steps and the four nameservers: change the nameservers.

Both depend on master and CloudFront still running, which they will until M2.

Top risks

  1. One operator, no backup. Every component in the table above with a named operator, except the legacy servers, has the same one. Access, credentials and the knowledge of these runbooks sit with one person.
  2. A personal Cloudflare account holds the zone, the Worker and the R2 bucket. The account migration is deferred, and nobody is named to own the new account.
  3. One host runs the sync, from dev checkouts. If onclappc02 is down, package updates stop reaching bioconductor.org and no failure issue is filed. The site keeps serving what is in R2.
  4. master is still in the path. It is the source of every package update. (/packages/stats/ no longer is: it is served from R2.) It retires only after M2.
  5. No rollback has been rehearsed. The steps above are written from the code and the cutover runbook. The DNS rollback target lasts only while the record freeze and the legacy servers do.
  6. Deploys are manual. The Worker and the registry deploy from a workstation with wrangler deploy; CD from CI is an open M0 item.
